meta.title: Who really said "When men, even unknowingly, are to meet one day, whatever may befall each, whatever the diverging paths, on the said day, they will inevitably come together in the red circle"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — the Buddha never said it. It is a fake epigraph invented by director Jean-Pierre Melville for his 1970 heist film Le Cercle Rouge.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When men, even unknowingly, are to meet one day, whatever may befall each, whatever the diverging paths, on the said day, they will inevitably come together in the red circle'?
meta.ogDescription: Not the Buddha. Jean-Pierre Melville fabricated this 'red circle' quote as the opening epigraph of his 1970 film Le Cercle Rouge.

answer.label: Not the Buddha — invented by Jean-Pierre Melville
answer.sourceLine: This is the opening epigraph of Melville’s 1970 heist film Le Cercle Rouge. On screen it is framed as the words of “Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha” and signed “Rama Krishna,” but Melville made the quote up himself ↗ — exactly as he had fabricated the fake samurai maxim opening Le Samouïrai. It appears in no Buddhist text.

source.heading: The real source: a film’s opening title card

docMeta.dd: Feature film — opening epigraph / title card

source.excerpt: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, drew a circle with a piece of red chalk and said: “When men, even unknowingly, are to meet one day, whatever may befall each, whatever the diverging paths, on the said day, they will inevitably come together in the red circle.”
trail: The 1970 film Le Cercle Rouge opens with this line, credited on screen to the Buddha and signed “Rama Krishna” (French Wikiquote transcript ↗).
Wikipedia’s article states the epigraph was one “Melville made up ↗,” noting he did the same with the invented maxim opening Le Samouïrai.
No such saying exists in the Pāli Canon or any Buddhist scripture; the “red circle” is a device Melville built for a film about fate drawing strangers together (Wikipedia ↗).
source.excerptNote: The epigraph as it appears at the start of the film. In the French title card the words are signed “Rama Krishna” even as they are put in the Buddha’s mouth — a doubled false attribution that is itself a clue the line is invented.
source.rightsHolder: Jean-Pierre Melville estate / the film’s rights holder (Studiocanal)
source.rightsNote: The line was written by Jean-Pierre Melville for Le Cercle Rouge, first shown in 1970 — well after 1931 — so both the original French text and its English rendering remain in copyright as part of the film. It is emphatically not an ancient public-domain Buddhist text.

author.name: Jean-Pierre Melville
author.heading: About Jean-Pierre Melville
author.bio: Jean-Pierre Melville (born Jean-Pierre Grumbach) was a French filmmaker whose spare, fatalistic crime films — Le Samouïrai, Le Cercle Rouge, Le Doulos — deeply influenced later directors from Scorsese to John Woo. He had a habit of opening his films with grave-sounding epigraphs attributed to Eastern sages, several of which he simply invented himself to set a mood of destiny and doom.

misattribution.heading: Why everyone thinks it’s the Buddha
misattribution.intro: The quote circulates as Buddhist wisdom because the film itself credits it to the Buddha — but that credit is part of the fiction.

items.why: The line is put in the Buddha’s mouth by the film’s title card, yet it corresponds to no sūtra or recorded teaching. Melville invented it ↗.

The French title card signs the words “Rama Krishna” (evoking the 19th-century mystic Ramakrishna), compounding the fiction; the Wikiquote transcript ↗ preserves that attribution without noting it is invented.
He used the same trick in Le Samouïrai (1967), opening with a fake “Bushido” maxim of his own writing — a known Melville signature move noted by Wikipedia ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The real author is French director Jean-Pierre Melville, who wrote the line for the 1970 title card of Le Cercle Rouge — not the Buddha (Wikipedia ↗).

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Melville’s film follows a thief, an escaped convict and a disgraced marksman who are strangers at the outset yet converge on a single Paris jewel heist. The invented “red circle” epigraph announces the theme — fate binding unacquainted men together — before a word of dialogue is spoken.
Because the line is grave, mystical and credited to the Buddha, it escaped the film and now travels social media as authentic Eastern wisdom, its cinematic origin forgotten.
context.pull: A screenwriter’s mood-setting device, not a sūtra.
